summary.text: For \(n=67\), two distinct inputs give the required residue sum: \(147\) yields \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67\), while \(2055\) yields \(1+3+7+8\cdot7=67\). Hence the multiplicity at \(67\) is at least two, rather than one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor \log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k)
\]
be the sequence A049802. Thus A383327 is
\[
a(n)=\#\{m:F(m)=n\}.
\]
To disprove the conjecture, it is enough to find one number in the displayed set for which the multiplicity is not one. We use the listed number \(n=67\), and exhibit two distinct indices at which A049802 has value \(67\).

First take \(m=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). Therefore
\[
F(147)=\sum_{k=1}^{7}(147\bmod 2^k).
\]
Now \(147=128+19\), and \(128\) is divisible by every \(2^k\) for \(1\le k\le 7\). Hence, over this range, the residue of \(147\) modulo \(2^k\) is the same as that of \(19\). The seven residues are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
k&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
147\bmod 2^k&1&3&3&3&19&19&19.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, \(19\equiv 1\pmod 2\), \(19\equiv3\pmod4\), \(19\equiv3\pmod8\), \(19\equiv3\pmod{16}\), and \(19<2^k\) for \(k=5,6,7\). Consequently,
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]

Next take \(m=2055\). Since
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\), and thus
\[
F(2055)=\sum_{k=1}^{11}(2055\bmod 2^k).
\]
Write \(2055=2048+7\). For every \(1\le k\le11\), the number \(2048=2^{11}\) is divisible by \(2^k\). The residues are therefore the residues of \(7\) modulo these powers of two. They are \(1\) modulo \(2\), \(3\) modulo \(4\), and \(7\) modulo every \(2^k\) with \(3\le k\le11\), because \(7<2^k\) in that range. There are nine integers \(k\) from \(3\) through \(11\), so
\[
F(2055)=1+3+9\cdot7=1+3+63=67.
\]

Thus A049802 takes the value \(67\) at each of the two distinct indices
\[
147\ne2055.
\]
It follows immediately that the number of occurrences of \(67\) in A049802 satisfies
\[
a(67)\ge2,
\]
and in particular \(a(67)\ne1\).

If the multiplicity is expressed using the finite search range in the stated definition, the same conclusion holds directly: both indices lie in that range, since
\[
147<2055<2^{12}<2^{68}=2^{67+1}.
\]
Hence the filtered set used to define \(a(67)\) contains at least the two distinct elements \(147\) and \(2055\), so its cardinality cannot be one.

Finally, \(67\) is one of
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
Therefore the assertion that \(a(n)=1\) for every \(n\) in this set fails at \(n=67\), which disproves the conjecture.
